clinicalPearls: Classic blood picture is a microcytic, hypochromic anemia (MCV <80 fL in established disease), but microcytosis can be ABSENT in early iron deficiency or masked by liver disease or concomitant folate/B12 deficiency (Harrison 22e p.765, p.450).

Low serum ferritin is the mainstay of absolute iron deficiency, reflecting depleted stores; ferritin <30 µg/L has high sensitivity and specificity (92% and 98%) and can be used as a single diagnostic test (Harrison 22e p.765).
Transferrin saturation (serum iron/TIBC) measures iron available for erythropoiesis; erythropoiesis becomes iron-restricted at values <15-20% (Harrison 22e p.765).

Anemia develops only in the LATE stage because the erythron is relatively spared compared with heart and skeletal muscle, which become iron-depleted earlier; slow progression plus compensation means anemia is often undetected, especially in the young, until hemoglobin falls below ~8 g/dL (Harrison 22e p.765).

Clinical clues include pica (compulsive ingestion of nonnutritive substances such as ice, soil, or clay), nail fragility and koilonychia, hair loss, cheilosis, atrophic glossitis, and dysphagia from esophageal webs (Plummer-Vinson syndrome) (Harrison 22e p.765; Koilonychia association noted p.~).

Even symptomatic isolated iron deficiency WITHOUT anemia matters: suboptimal myocyte, cardiomyocyte, and neuron function can cause fatigue, irritability, poor concentration, restless legs syndrome, and reduced exercise capacity (Harrison 22e p.765).

Severe iron-deficiency anemia may be accompanied by thrombocytosis, due to prevalent megakaryocyte commitment of the common erythroid-platelet progenitor when iron is insufficient (Harrison 22e p.766).
Serum hepcidin is low/undetectable in absolute iron deficiency (maximizing dietary iron absorption) but elevated in inflammation and in IRIDA (TMPRSS6 mutations) (Harrison 22e p.766).

Inadequate therapeutic response (no reticulocytosis after 1 week, or <1 g/dL hemoglobin rise after 2 weeks of iron therapy) should prompt a search for the cause: noncompliance, ongoing blood loss, or malabsorption (Harrison 22e p.766).
harrison.pathophysiology: Iron supply becomes inadequate for needs through excessive demand, insufficient intake, defective absorption, or blood loss; multiple causes frequently co-occur, especially in the elderly and in multimorbidity (Harrison 22e p.764). In ISOLATED iron deficiency, stores are depleted while hemoglobin is still normal; when iron remains sufficient for erythropoiesis, red cells are normochromic/normocytic with decreased ferritin (<15-30 µg/L). As transferrin saturation falls <15-20%, iron supply to erythropoiesis is insufficient and cells become hypochromic and microcytic, the classic feature of iron-deficiency anemia (Harrison 22e p.764). Iron deficiency is ABSOLUTE when stores are exhausted and FUNCTIONAL when erythropoiesis is iron-restricted but stores are adequate or even increased. Low hepcidin in iron deficiency maximizes dietary absorption; TMPRSS6 mutations cause hereditary iron-refractory IDA (IRIDA) with reduced absorption and oral-iron refractoriness. In inflammation, high hepcidin sequesters iron into stores, producing functional iron deficiency with low serum iron and transferrin saturation despite elevated ferritin; absolute and functional deficiency often coexist (IBD, CKD, aging). Beyond anemia, heart, muscle, and brain are affected; immune response may be blunted as lymphocytes require iron during the metabolic burst (Harrison 22e p.764).
additionalDifferentials: Anemia of inflammation (anemia of chronic disease) - the second most common anemia worldwide, due to functional iron deficiency; a diagnosis of exclusion usually occurring with an inflammatory disorder such as cancer or infection (Harrison 22e p.765, p.450).
Thalassemia trait - microcytosis with normal-to-high ferritin and serum iron; red cells are more homogeneous in volume with a low/normal RDW (Harrison 22e p.450, p.767).
Mixed forms (combined absolute and functional iron deficiency) (Harrison 22e p.767).
Other nutritional anemias - vitamin B12 and folate deficiency (megaloblastic, macrocytic); may coexist with and mask iron deficiency in malabsorption (Harrison 22e p.765).
Sideroblastic anemia (rare) as a cause of microcytic hypochromic red cells (Harrison 22e p.~).
nonInfectiousMimics: Anemia of inflammation / chronic disease (functional iron deficiency from high hepcidin: low serum iron and transferrin saturation with NORMAL-to-HIGH ferritin) (Harrison 22e p.764, p.767).
Thalassemia trait (microcytic but with normal-to-high ferritin and iron, and a low/normal RDW) (Harrison 22e p.450, p.767).
additionalInvestigations: Serum ferritin (mainstay; <30 µg/L diagnostic, sensitivity 92% / specificity 98%); note ferritin is an acute-phase reactant and may rise severalfold in inflammation (Harrison 22e p.765, p.450).
Transferrin saturation (serum iron/TIBC); iron-restricted erythropoiesis at <15-20% (Harrison 22e p.765).
Serum iron (reduced, but diurnal fluctuation prevents use as a single test) (Harrison 22e p.765).
MCV and RDW from the CBC (MCV <80 fL when established; RDW often elevated reflecting anisocytosis) (Harrison 22e p.765).
Soluble transferrin receptor (sTfR) - increased in iron deficiency; sTfR/log ferritin ratio >2 favors iron deficiency (Harrison 22e p.766, p.767).
Reticulocyte hemoglobin content (CHr, reduced) and percentage of hypochromic red cells (%HYPO, increased >6%), reflecting iron availability days to months before testing (Harrison 22e p.766, p.767).
Serum hepcidin (low/undetectable in absolute deficiency; not routinely measured, reference values not standardized) (Harrison 22e p.766, p.767).
Absence of stainable iron in bone marrow remains the gold standard, although it is rarely needed and unacceptably invasive (Harrison 22e p.765).
Endoscopy and/or radiographic imaging to identify the cause - essential in males and postmenopausal females to rule out malignancy or other severe bleeding sources (Harrison 22e p.765, p.~).
redFlags: Unexplained iron-deficiency anemia in any adult (with the possible exception of a premenopausal, multiparous woman) MANDATES thorough endoscopic and/or radiographic visualization of the entire large bowel - right (ascending) colon cancer causes insidious blood loss and often presents as IDA (Harrison 22e p.~, colorectal cancer chapter).
Imaging and endoscopy to trace the cause are essential in males and postmenopausal females to rule out malignancy or other severe causes of bleeding (Harrison 22e p.765).
Hemoglobin falling below ~8 g/dL or otherwise severe anemia (Harrison 22e p.765).

Myelophthisic blood smear (nucleated red cells, teardrop cells, immature white cells) suggesting marrow infiltration mandates marrow examination - a competing cause of anemia to recognize (Harrison 22e p.450).
harrison.prognosis: Iron deficiency and IDA are highly treatable with iron replacement. Oral iron usually requires at least ~3 months of therapy to restore hemoglobin and replenish stores and prevent early recurrence; inadequate response (no reticulocytosis at 1 week or <1 g/dL hemoglobin rise at 2 weeks) should prompt a search for noncompliance, ongoing blood loss, or malabsorption. Prognosis ultimately depends on the underlying cause (e.g., occult GI malignancy) rather than the anemia itself (Harrison 22e p.766).
pitfalls: Classic microcytosis/hypochromia can be ABSENT in early iron deficiency, in elderly patients, or when masked by concomitant folate/B12 deficiency or liver disease - do not exclude IDA on a normal MCV alone (Harrison 22e p.765, p.450).
Ferritin is an acute-phase reactant; normal or high ferritin during inflammation can mask coexisting iron deficiency (Harrison 22e p.450).
Serum iron alone is unreliable as a single test due to diurnal variation (Harrison 22e p.765).
Treating IDA without investigating the cause can miss occult GI malignancy; isolated symptomatic iron deficiency without anemia should not be underestimated (Harrison 22e p.764, p.765).
Biomarkers other than ferritin and transferrin saturation are limited by poor standardization and accessibility (Harrison 22e p.766).
harrison.severityClassification: Harrison describes a continuum rather than a formal grading scale: (1) isolated/absolute iron deficiency with depleted stores (ferritin <15-30 µg/L) but NORMAL hemoglobin and normochromic-normocytic cells; (2) iron-restricted erythropoiesis once transferrin saturation falls <15-20%, with hypochromic microcytic cells; (3) overt iron-deficiency anemia. Severe anemia is generally taken as hemoglobin <=8 g/dL (the threshold at which anemia commonly becomes detectable and at which rapid IV correction is considered) (Harrison 22e p.764-766).
